Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 1.5 is quoted verbatim in a quote environment; it is an external theorem node linked by specializes edges to the polygon-level results that formalise its parts, and the Coleman--Mazur--Buzzard--Kilford conjecture resolves to it.
The summability-of-minors paragraph justifies a claim made inside the definition of the Fredholm determinant; with no separate result to prove it is a remark rather than a proof.

The dependency-ledger table of the last section, the discussion paragraphs (a)-(c) on what Theorem 1.5 says, and the informal descriptions of LWX Theorems 1.3/1.5 in the chapter introduction are not extracted as nodes.

nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a normed ring, $\sigma$ an index type and $c : \sigma \to \R$. A power series $f = \sum_t a_t x^t \in R[[x_i : i \in \sigma]]$ is \emph{restricted for $c$} if \[ \lVert a_t \rVert \prod_{i} c_i^{\,t_i} \longrightarrow 0 \] along the cofinite filter on the multidegrees $t$.
nodes.name: Restricted power series
nodes.statement_short: A multivariate power series is restricted for radius $c$ when its weighted coefficients tend to 0 along the cofinite filter.
differentia: \lVert a_t \rVert \prod_{i} c_i^{\,t_i} \longrightarrow 0 \] along the cofinite filter on the multidegrees $t$
also_stated_at: A power series satisfying this is called \emph{restricted} for $c$, and the collection of them is the ring we work in.
nodes.label: def:isrestricted

nodes.statement: $f$ is restricted for $c$ if and only if it is restricted for $\lvert c \rvert$.
nodes.name: Restrictedness depends only on |c|
conclusions: $f$ is restricted for $c$ if and only if it is restricted for $\lvert c \rvert$
nodes.label: lem:isrestricted-abs

nodes.statement: The restricted series for a fixed $c$ form a subring of $R[[x_i]]$. We write $R_c\langle x_i : i \in \sigma\rangle$, or $\mathrm{Restricted}\ R\ c$, for it.

nodes.statement: Closure under subtraction is the usual squeeze. Multiplication is the interesting axiom: the coefficients of a product are antidiagonal sums, \[ (fg)_t = \sum_{u + w = t} a_u b_w , \] and it is not immediate that these tend to $0$. They do, because for each $t$ the antidiagonal is finite and the norm of the sum is bounded by the maximum of $\lVert a_u \rVert c^u \cdot \lVert b_w \rVert c^w$ over it; given $\varepsilon$, all but finitely many $u$ have $\lVert a_u\rVert c^u$ small and all but finitely many $w$ have $\lVert b_w \rVert c^w$ small, and a multidegree $t$ outside a suitable finite set cannot be split with both parts in the exceptional sets.

nodes.statement: The \emph{Gauss norm} of $f$ at radius $c$ is \[ \lVert f \rVert_c = \sup_t \; \lVert a_t \rVert \prod_i c_i^{\,t_i}, \] when the supremum is finite; the predicate $\mathrm{HasGaussNorm}$ records finiteness.

nodes.statement: Let $f, g$ be restricted with nonzero Gauss norms. Fix any well-order on $\sigma$ and let $u$, $w$ be the achieving multidegrees of $f$ and $g$ that are largest for the induced lexicographic order. Then the term $a_u b_w$ strictly dominates every other term of the antidiagonal of $u + w$.
nodes.name: Dominant terms on the antidiagonal

nodes.statement: Any other splitting $u' + w' = u + w$ has $u' \neq u$, so by maximality either $u'$ is not achieving --- and then its term is strictly smaller --- or $u'$ is achieving and lexicographically smaller, forcing $w'$ to be lexicographically larger than $w$ and hence non-achieving. Either way one factor is strictly below its Gauss norm.

nodes.statement_short: Maximality of the chosen achieving multidegrees forces one factor strictly below its Gauss norm.

nodes.statement: A Cauchy sequence is coefficientwise Cauchy, since each coefficient functional is norm-nonincreasing, so the coefficients converge in $R$ and assemble into a candidate limit. Convergence in Gauss norm then follows from the same uniform estimate.

nodes.statement: If $\lVert f - C(f_0)\rVert_c < \lVert f_0 \rVert$ then $f = C(f_0)(1 + \delta)$ with $\lVert \delta \rVert_c < 1$, and $1 + \delta$ is invertible by the geometric series, which converges by Theorem~\ref{thm:restricted-complete}. nodes.statement: Let $f \in A_c\langle T \rangle$ and $s \in \N$. nodes.statement_short: A restricted series is distinguished of order $s$ if $f_s$ is a multiplicative unit whose Gauss term attains the norm and strictly dominates all later Gauss terms.
nodes.label: def:ismuldistinguished

Let $g$ be distinguished of order $s$ and let $q \in A_c\langle T\rangle$ be nonzero. Then \[ \lVert g q \rVert_c = \lVert g \rVert_c \lVert q \rVert_c, \] and the product achieves its Gauss norm at the index $s + k_0(q)$, and at no larger index.

nodes.statement: The coefficient of $T^{s + k_0}$ in $gq$ is $g_s q_{k_0} + \sum_{i + j = s + k_0, \, i \neq s} g_i q_j$. The ultrametric equality case gives the claim, and the same estimate applied at larger indices gives the maximality.

nodes.statement: A \emph{one-sided polygon} over an ordered value group $\Gamma$ consists of a starting vertex in $\Z \times \Gamma$, a sequence of segment lengths, and a monotone sequence of slopes, together with the bookkeeping that says where the polygon stops (it may be finite, may end in a ray, or may continue forever). Monotonicity of the slopes is convexity, built into the structure rather than imposed afterwards.
nodes.name: One-sided polygon
nodes.label: def:newtonpolygon0

nodes.statement: A one-sided polygon $P$ is \emph{the Newton polygon of} $v$ when \begin{enumerate} \item there are no points of $v$ strictly left of the starting vertex, and the starting vertex is itself a point of $v$; \item $P$ lies on or below every point: $P(k) \leq v_k$ for all $k \in \N$; and \item $P$ is the greatest such: any polygon $Q$ with the same starting abscissa lying on or below every point lies on or below $P$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.name: Newton polygon (specification)
nodes.statement_short: The Newton polygon of $v$ is the greatest polygon anchored at a point of $v$ lying on or below every point of $v$.
nodes.label: def:isnewtonpolygonof

nodes.statement: Two polygons satisfying Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof} for the same $v$ have the same height at every integer.

nodes.statement: A \emph{Banach--Tate ring} is a complete normed ring $R$ possessing a \emph{pseudo-uniformizer}: a unit $\varpi$ with $\lVert \varpi \rVert < 1$ whose norm is multiplicative. We write $\mathrm{IsTate}\, R$.
nodes.name: Banach--Tate ring
nodes.label: def:istate

nodes.statement: For an index type $I$ the \emph{model space} $c(I, R)$ is the space of families $(x_i)_{i \in I}$ in $R$ tending to $0$ along the cofinite filter, with the supremum norm.
nodes.name: Model space c(I,R)
nodes.label: def:cspace

nodes.statement: A Banach $R$-module $M$ is \emph{orthonormalisable} if it is isometrically isomorphic to some $c(I,R)$, and has \emph{property (Pr)} if it is a direct summand of an orthonormalisable module.

nodes.name: Matrix coefficient and row norm
nodes.label: def:matrixcoeff

nodes.statement: $u$ is \emph{completely continuous} if it is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, and \emph{compactoid} if its row norms tend to $0$ along the cofinite filter.

nodes.statement: On $c(I,R)$ the two notions agree, and a row-decay estimate $\lVert u_{ji} \rVert \leq C \sigma^{j}$ with $\sigma < 1$ suffices for both.

a row-decay estimate $\lVert u_{ji} \rVert \leq C \sigma^{j}$ with $\sigma < 1$ suffices for both

A subgroup $U \subseteq D_f^\times$ has \emph{wild level $\geq \gamma$} if $\mathrm{toMatrix}_v(U) \subseteq \Sigma_0(\gamma)$; this is Buzzard's condition \cite[\S9]{Buzzard}, and $\Delta = \mathrm{toMatrix}_v^{-1}(\Sigma_0(\gamma))$ is the monoid on which the weight will act.

$\mathrm{LevelBounds}\, S\, \rho$ records the norm estimates extracted from an acting monoid $S$: entries integral, $\lVert c \rVert \leq \rho$, and $\lVert d \rVert = 1$.
nodes.name: Level bounds
nodes.label: def:levelbounds

nodes.statement: A \emph{weight datum} $W$ at $(S, \rho)$ consists of the level bounds, the expansion $\kappa\mathrm{col}(c,d) \in K[[z]]$ of $\kappa(cz+d)$ as a function of the lower row, the decay estimate $\lVert \mathrm{coeff}_m \rVert \leq \rho^m$, absolute summability, and the cocycle identity making $\|_\kappa$ an action.
nodes.name: Weight datum
nodes.label: def:weightseries

nodes.statement: An \emph{analytic weight} is a genuine character $\kappa : U_K \to K^\times$ together with an expansion datum for it. The expansion is unique on the level, so the pair is no more data than the character; but carrying it makes the weight action a definition rather than a choice.
nodes.name: Analytic weight
nodes.label: def:analyticweight

nodes.statement: $\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g)$ is the continuous $K$-linear operator on the Tate algebra determined by $z^k \mapsto \kappa(cz+d)(cz+d)^{-2}\left(\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\right)^k$.
nodes.name: kappa-slash operator
nodes.label: def:kappaslash

nodes.statement: Under the identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:tate-algebra-onable}, the matrix of $\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g)$ is the coefficient array of the two-variable generating function $\kappa\mathrm{col}\cdot(cx+d)^{-1}(cx+d-axy-by)^{-1}$; and if $\lVert a \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma$ then \[ \lVert \mathrm{matrixCoeff}(\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g))_{j i} \rVert \leq \sigma^{\,j}. \]
nodes.name: Matrix of the weight action and row decay
nodes.statement_short: The weight-action matrix is a generating-function coefficient array whose $j$-th row decays like $\sigma^j$.
assumptions: if $\lVert a \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma$
conclusions: \lVert \mathrm{matrixCoeff}(\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(g))_{j i} \rVert \leq \sigma^{\,j}
nodes.label: prop:kappaslash-matrix

nodes.statement: Let $\theta$ be the component map, $S$ an acting monoid, $\kappa$ an analytic weight, $U$ a subgroup with $\theta(U) \subseteq S$, and $\chi$ a twisting character. Then \[ S_\kappa(U) = \left\{ \varphi : D_f^\times \to K\langle z\rangle \;:\; \varphi(dgu) = \chi(u_v)\, \varphi(g) \|_\kappa u_v \ \ \forall d \in \Gamma,\ u \in U \right\}. \]
nodes.name: Quaternionic modular forms S_kappa(U)
nodes.label: def:forms

nodes.statement: For $\eta$ in the acting monoid, write $U \eta U = \coprod_i U x_i$ and set $[U\eta U]\varphi = \sum_i \varphi \|_\kappa x_i$. This is independent of the representatives and preserves $S_\kappa(U)$.
nodes.name: Double coset (Hecke) operator
nodes.label: def:heckeoperator

nodes.statement: If $U$ is open and compact then $U \eta U$ is a finite union of right cosets of $U$.
nodes.name: Finiteness of double cosets
assumptions: If $U$ is open and compact
conclusions: $U \eta U$ is a finite union of right cosets of $U$
nodes.label: thm:hecke-finiteness

nodes.statement: The standard levels are compact open. Concretely: the units of a compact multiplicatively closed set form a compact set of units, because $u \mapsto (u, u^{-1})$ is a closed embedding; and the integral order $\calO_D \otimes \Zhat \subseteq D_f$ is compact, being the image of a product of compact local integer rings under a continuous coordinate map.
nodes.name: Standard levels are compact open
conclusions: The standard levels are compact open
nodes.label: prop:compact-open-levels

nodes.statement: For $U$ open the class set $\Gamma \backslash D_f^\times / U$ is finite.
nodes.name: Fujisaki's lemma
assumptions: For $U$ open
conclusions: the class set $\Gamma \backslash D_f^\times / U$ is finite
nodes.label: thm:fujisaki

nodes.name: Class-set representatives and stabilisers
nodes.statement: Fix representatives $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of the class set and let $\Gamma_i = c_i^{-1}\Gamma c_i \cap U$ be the stabilisers.
$\mathrm{evalAtReps}(\varphi) = (\varphi(c_i))_i$, a map $S_\kappa(U) \to c(\iota \times \N, K)$.
nodes.name: Evaluation at representatives
nodes.label: def:evalatreps

nodes.statement: $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ is injective, and its image is exactly the tuples whose $i$-th block is $\Gamma_i$-invariant. If the level is \emph{neat} --- every $\Gamma_i$ acts trivially on the Tate algebra --- it is bijective, so $S_\kappa(U) \cong c(\iota \times \N, K)$.
nodes.name: Evaluation at representatives is injective
conclusions: $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ is injective, and its image is exactly the tuples whose $i$-th block is $\Gamma_i$-invariant
If the level is \emph{neat} --- every $\Gamma_i$ acts trivially on the Tate algebra --- it is bijective, so $S_\kappa(U) \cong c(\iota \times \N, K)$
nodes.label: thm:evalatreps

nodes.statement: Given right coset representatives $v_t$ of $U\eta U$ and, for each $(i,t)$, a factorisation $c_i v_t^{-1} = d_{i,t}\, c_{\sigma(i,t)}\, u_{i,t}$ with $d_{i,t} \in \Gamma$, $u_{i,t} \in U$, the $(i,j)$ \emph{block} is \[ \varepsilon_{ij} = \sum_{t \,:\, \sigma(i,t) = j} \chi(w_{i,t})\, \kappa\text{-}\mathrm{slash}(w_{i,t}), \qquad w_{i,t} = \theta(u_{i,t} v_t), \] and $\mathrm{heckeBlockOp}$ is the operator on $c(\iota \times \N, K)$ they assemble.
nodes.name: Hecke block operator
nodes.label: def:heckeblock

nodes.statement: $\bigl([U\eta U]\varphi\bigr)(c_i) = \sum_j \varepsilon_{ij}\bigl(\varphi(c_j)\bigr)$; that is, $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ intertwines $[U\eta U]$ with $\mathrm{heckeBlockOp}$.
nodes.name: The transport
conclusions: $\mathrm{evalAtReps}$ intertwines $[U\eta U]$ with $\mathrm{heckeBlockOp}$
nodes.label: thm:transport

nodes.statement: Suppose $\lVert \det \theta(\eta) \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma < 1$. Then every block, and hence the block operator, is compactoid.
nodes.name: Compactness of the Hecke block operator
assumptions: Suppose $\lVert \det \theta(\eta) \rVert \leq \sigma$ with $\rho \leq \sigma < 1$
conclusions: every block, and hence the block operator, is compactoid
nodes.label: thm:qmf-compact

nodes.statement: Each certificate element $u_{i,t}v_t$ has determinant norm at most that of $\eta$, the outer factors being integral; a small determinant with integral entries and unit $d$ forces $\lVert a \rVert \leq \sigma$; and then Proposition~\ref{prop:kappaslash-matrix} gives the row decay $\sigma^j$, which is Proposition~\ref{prop:compactoid-criterion}'s hypothesis. A finite sum of compactoid operators is compactoid.
nodes.name: Proof of Compactness of the Hecke block operator
nodes.statement_short: Small determinant forces small $a$; Proposition on kappa-slash gives row decay; finite sums.

nodes.statement: $\det(1 - T\,[U\eta U])$, computed in the block model.
nodes.name: Hecke Fredholm determinant
nodes.label: def:heckecharpowerseries

nodes.statement: At a neat level, $a \neq 0$ is a zero of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$ if and only if $a^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $[U\eta U]$ on $S_\kappa(U)$.
nodes.name: Eigenforms are reciprocal roots
assumptions: At a neat level
conclusions: $a \neq 0$ is a zero of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$ if and only if $a^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $[U\eta U]$ on $S_\kappa(U)$
equivalent_conditions: $a \neq 0$ is a zero of $\det(1 - T[U\eta U])$
$a^{-1}$ is an eigenvalue of $[U\eta U]$ on $S_\kappa(U)$
nodes.label: thm:qmf-eigenform-criterion

nodes.statement: Each zero $a$ of the determinant, of multiplicity $n$, gives a decomposition $S_\kappa(U) = N \oplus F$ into $[U\eta U]$-stable summands with $(1 - a[U\eta U])^n = 0$ on $N$, invertible on $F$, and $\dim_K N = n$.
nodes.name: Riesz decomposition for quaternionic forms
assumptions: Each zero $a$ of the determinant, of multiplicity $n$
conclusions: gives a decomposition $S_\kappa(U) = N \oplus F$ into $[U\eta U]$-stable summands with $(1 - a[U\eta U])^n = 0$ on $N$, invertible on $F$, and $\dim_K N = n$
nodes.label: thm:qmf-riesz

nodes.statement: Without neatness, averaging over the finite stabilisers gives projectors realising $S_\kappa(U)$ as a direct summand of the model, so it satisfies property (Pr). The determinant of $[U\eta U]$ on the summand is well defined and independent of the projector chosen \cite[Lemma 2.12]{Buzzard}.
nodes.name: Non-neat levels satisfy property (Pr)
assumptions: Without neatness
conclusions: averaging over the finite stabilisers gives projectors realising $S_\kappa(U)$ as a direct summand of the model, so it satisfies property (Pr)
The determinant of $[U\eta U]$ on the summand is well defined and independent of the projector chosen
nodes.label: prop:pr

nodes.statement: If $\kappa'$ over $L$ is compatible with $\kappa$ over $K$ along an isometric embedding $K \to L$, then the two determinants correspond \cite[Lemma 2.13]{Buzzard}. This is what lets a computation made over a small field be read over $\bbC_p$.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.name: Base change of the Hecke determinant
assumptions: If $\kappa'$ over $L$ is compatible with $\kappa$ over $K$ along an isometric embedding $K \to L$
conclusions: the two determinants correspond
nodes.label: prop:qmf-basechange

nodes.name: Commuting Hecke algebra taken as data
nodes.statement: Following Buzzard \cite[\S5]{Buzzard} we take the commuting structure of the Hecke algebra as data rather than proving it; for $T_w, T_{w'}$ at distinct places it is a Satake computation outside our scope.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra

nodes.statement: Two double coset operators commute as soon as their representative families can be matched pairwise, up to the level, with the two products taken in the opposite orders.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.name: Commutation criterion for double coset operators
conclusions: Two double coset operators commute as soon as their representative families can be matched pairwise, up to the level, with the two products taken in the opposite orders
nodes.label: prop:hecke-comm-criterion

nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{T}$ be a commuting family of endomorphisms of $S_\kappa(U)$, each commuting with $\varphi = [U\eta U]$, and let $N$ be the finite-slope subspace of Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-riesz}. Then every element of $\mathbb{T}$ preserves $N$, and over an algebraically closed coefficient field $N$ contains a nonzero simultaneous generalised eigenvector: a $\varphi$-finite system of eigenvalues.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.name: Finite-slope systems of eigenvalues
assumptions: Let $\mathbb{T}$ be a commuting family of endomorphisms of $S_\kappa(U)$, each commuting with $\varphi = [U\eta U]$
let $N$ be the finite-slope subspace of Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-riesz}
conclusions: every element of $\mathbb{T}$ preserves $N$
over an algebraically closed coefficient field $N$ contains a nonzero simultaneous generalised eigenvector
nodes.label: prop:qmf-eigensystem

nodes.statement: Stability is the identity $(1-a\varphi)^n t = t (1-a\varphi)^n$ applied to a vector killed by the left factor. $N$ is finite dimensional by Theorem~\ref{thm:qmf-riesz} and nonzero, and a commuting family of endomorphisms of a nonzero finite-dimensional space over an algebraically closed field is simultaneously triangularisable.
nodes.section: 6.7 Base change and the Hecke algebra
nodes.name: Proof of Finite-slope systems of eigenvalues
nodes.statement_short: Commutation identity for stability; simultaneous triangularisation on finite-dimensional $N$.

nodes.name: Row-weight decay
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a compactoid operator whose matrix decays along a row weight $w$, meaning $\lVert u_{ji} \rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds

nodes.statement: If $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$ for all $i, j$ then $\lVert \mathrm{minor}(u, S) \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_{j \in S} w_j}$ for every finite $S$.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.name: Minor bound from row decay
assumptions: If $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$ for all $i, j$
conclusions: $\lVert \mathrm{minor}(u, S) \rVert \leq \sigma^{\sum_{j \in S} w_j}$ for every finite $S$
nodes.label: lem:minor-bound

nodes.statement: Let $0 \leq \sigma < 1$, let $u$ be compactoid with $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$, and let $f : \N \to \N$ satisfy $f(n) \leq \sum_{j \in S} w_j$ for every $S$ with $\lvert S \rvert = n$. Then \[ \lVert c_n(u) \rVert \leq \sigma^{f(n)} . \]
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.name: The slope bound
assumptions: Let $0 \leq \sigma < 1$
let $u$ be compactoid with $\lVert u_{ji}\rVert \leq \sigma^{w_j}$
let $f : \N \to \N$ satisfy $f(n) \leq \sum_{j \in S} w_j$ for every $S$ with $\lvert S \rvert = n$
conclusions: \lVert c_n(u) \rVert \leq \sigma^{f(n)}
nodes.label: thm:slope-bound

nodes.statement: $c_n$ is $\pm$ the sum of the $n$-element minors, and an ultrametric infinite sum is bounded by the supremum of its terms; each term is bounded by Lemma~\ref{lem:minor-bound} and then by $\sigma^{f(n)}$ since $\sigma \leq 1$ and $f(n)$ is the smaller exponent.
nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds
nodes.name: Proof of The slope bound
nodes.statement_short: Ultrametric sum bounded by its largest term, each bounded by the minor bound.

nodes.statement: Among $n$-element subsets of $\N$, the sum $\sum_{i \in S} i$ is minimised uniquely by $S = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, with value $\binom{n}{2}$; every other $n$-element subset has sum at least $\binom{n}{2} + 1$.

conclusions: the sum $\sum_{i \in S} i$ is minimised uniquely by $S = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, with value $\binom{n}{2}$
every other $n$-element subset has sum at least $\binom{n}{2} + 1$

nodes.section: 7.1 From row decay to coefficient bounds

assumptions: On $\iota \times \N$ with $\lvert \iota \rvert = d$ and weight $(i, m) \mapsto m$
conclusions: an $n$-element subset has weight sum at least $\sum_{k < n} \lfloor k/d \rfloor$

nodes.statement: Let $D = \bbH_{\Q}$ be Hamilton's quaternions over $\Q$, a definite quaternion algebra of discriminant $2$; let $v_3$ be the place above $3$ and $K_3 = \Q_3$ its completion. Since $3 \nmid 2$, $D$ splits at $v_3$, and a splitting is fixed by choosing a square root $\nu$ of $-2$ in $K_3$; the resulting isomorphism $\theta_3 : D \otimes_{\Q} K_3 \cong M_2(K_3)$ is the rigidification of Definition~\ref{def:rigidification}.
nodes.name: Jacobs's setting: Hamilton quaternions at 3
nodes.label: def:jacobs-setting

nodes.statement: The \emph{Hurwitz order} is $\calO = \Z\langle i, j, \tfrac12(1+i+j+k)\rangle \subseteq \bbH_{\Q}$, the unique maximal order up to conjugacy. We record membership by the parity condition that $2x$ has integer coordinates all of the same parity.
nodes.name: Hurwitz order
nodes.label: def:hurwitz

nodes.statement: A Hurwitz quaternion is a unit exactly when its reduced norm is $1$, and $\calO^\times$ has exactly $24$ elements.
nodes.name: Hurwitz units
conclusions: A Hurwitz quaternion is a unit exactly when its reduced norm is $1$
$\calO^\times$ has exactly $24$ elements
nodes.label: prop:hurwitz-units

nodes.statement: $U_0(1) \subseteq D_f^\times$ consists of the adelic units integral at every finite place --- the unit group of $\calO \otimes \Zhat$ --- and $U_1(9)$ refines it by the congruence $\theta_3(g) \equiv \left(\begin{smallmatrix} * & * \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ modulo $9$.
nodes.name: Levels U_0(1) and U_1(9)
nodes.label: def:jacobs-levels

nodes.statement: $U_0(1)$ and $U_1(9)$ are compact open, so Theorem~\ref{thm:hecke-finiteness} applies and the Hecke operators at this level are defined without exhibiting representatives.
nodes.name: U_0(1) and U_1(9) are compact open
conclusions: $U_0(1)$ and $U_1(9)$ are compact open
nodes.label: prop:jacobs-levels-compact-open

nodes.statement: The everywhere-integral elements of $D \otimes \A_f$ are exactly the $\Zhat$-span of the Hurwitz basis $1, i, j, \omega$: one inclusion is clear, and the other extracts each coordinate by a $\Q$-linear functional, extends it to the completion, and uses that a rational integral at every finite place is a rational integer. That set is compact by Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-open-levels} and open because the integral adeles are open, so $U_0(1)$ is compact open; $U_1(9)$ is cut out of it by a congruence condition at $3$, which is clopen because closed balls in an ultrametric field are open.
nodes.name: Proof of U_0(1) and U_1(9) are compact open
nodes.statement_short: Integral elements are the Zhat-span of the Hurwitz basis; compact and open.

nodes.statement: $D_f^\times = D^\times \cdot U_0(1)$, and the class set at level $U_1(9)$ has exactly three elements, represented by explicit adelic $c_0, c_1, c_2$.

nodes.statement: Class number one for the Hurwitz order is classical; formalised here by the idelic dictionary, reducing a global integrality statement to local approximation. Passing from $U_0(1)$ to $U_1(9)$ replaces the class set by the orbits of $\calO^\times$ on the primitive vectors of $(\Z/9)^2$, which are computed to be three.

nodes.statement: A power series $F = \sum a_n T^n$ over a normed ring $R$ is \emph{entire} if $\lVert a_n\rVert C^n \to 0$ for every $C > 0$; equivalently, if it is restricted at every radius in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:isrestricted}. nodes.statement: Let $g \in R[T]$ have invertible leading coefficient and degree $n$. Every entire $F$ can be written uniquely as $F = g\,q + r$ with $q$ entire and $r$ a polynomial of degree $< n$.

nodes.statement: Existence and uniqueness are Martin's Weierstrass division (Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision} and Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision-unique}) applied at a radius large enough that $g$ dominates: the divisor of a distinguished division is precisely a polynomial whose leading coefficient achieves the Gauss norm, and for a polynomial with invertible leading coefficient this happens at all sufficiently large radii. Entireness of the quotient is then the statement that the division is performed at every radius simultaneously, which uniqueness supplies.
nodes.name: Proof of Euclidean division in R{{T}}
nodes.statement_short: Martin's Weierstrass division at large radii; entireness by uniqueness.

nodes.statement: An entire $F$ has a \emph{good zero of order $s$} at $a$ if the divided derivatives $\Delta^{i}F$ vanish at $a$ for $i < s$ and $\Delta^{s}F(a)$ is a unit (\cite[Definition II.2.11]{Bellaiche}). nodes.statement: Bella\"iche and Kedlaya \cite[Proposition 3.2.2]{Kedlaya} both run a Newton iteration $P_{l+1} = P_l + X_l$, $Q_{l+1} = Q_l + Y_l$ driven by the division estimates $\lVert f\rVert = \max(\lVert g\rVert\lVert q\rVert, \lVert r\rVert)$. We instead observe that those division estimates \emph{are} Martin's, so the hypotheses say exactly that $F$ is distinguished of order $N$ at radius $\rho$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dominant-distinguished}); dividing $T^N$ by $F$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:wdivision}) and subtracting the remainder from $T^N$ produces the monic factor. This is Weierstrass preparation (Theorem~\ref{thm:wprep}) in the form needed. For coprimality (the norm-level form of \cite[Lemma 2.2.7]{JN}, and where \cite{JN} argue with resultants over the Gelfand spectrum): $\lVert G-1\rVert_\rho < 1$, so $G$ is a unit of the Tate algebra of radius $\rho$; dividing $G^{-1}$ by $P$ there gives $1 = Pq' + rG$ with $\deg r < N$, and the cofactor is entire because the entire division of $1 - rG$ by $P$ has the same quotient, by uniqueness. That is a B\'ezout identity for $P$ and $G$ in $R\{\{T\}\}$.

conclusions: $\lVert c_n(u)\rVert \leq \sigma^{f(n)}$ whenever $f(n) \leq \sum_{a\in S} w(a) - \sum_{a \in S} w'(a)$ for all $\lvert S\rvert = n$
nodes.label: lem:two-sided

nodes.statement: A permutation $\pi$ of $S$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in S} w'(\pi a) = \sum_{a \in S} w'(a)$, so every Leibniz monomial of $\mathrm{minor}(u,S)$ carries the same column contribution and the row contribution is $\sum_{a\in S}w(a)$. This is the Hadamard bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard} with the column weight subtracted; note that nothing is inverted, so the estimate runs over an arbitrary complete ultrametric ring rather than a field.
nodes.name: Proof of Two-sided weight bounds
nodes.statement_short: Column contributions are permutation-invariant; Hadamard bound with column weight subtracted.

nodes.statement: If $D\,M_v = M_u\,D$ entrywise for a diagonal $D$ with unit entries then $\mathrm{minor}(v,S) = \mathrm{minor}(u,S)$ for every finite $S$, and hence $\det(1-Tv) = \det(1-Tu)$. No compactness hypothesis and no inversion of $D$ is needed.
nodes.name: Diagonal intertwining
assumptions: If $D\,M_v = M_u\,D$ entrywise for a diagonal $D$ with unit entries
conclusions: $\mathrm{minor}(v,S) = \mathrm{minor}(u,S)$ for every finite $S$
$\det(1-Tv) = \det(1-Tu)$
nodes.label: lem:diag-intertwine

nodes.statement: An operator $f$ on $c(I,R)$ induces the block-diagonal operator $\mathrm{blockDiag}\,f$ on $c(\sigma\times I, R)$, an equivalence if $f$ is; more generally a map $f : c(I,R) \to c(I',R)$ changing the fibre induces $\mathrm{blockMap}\,f$, and a family $T_{ij} : c(I,R)\to c(I',R)$ induces the rectangular block operator $\mathrm{blockOpMap}\,T$, with the expected composition rules against Proposition~\ref{prop:blockop}.
nodes.name: Block-diagonal and rectangular block maps
nodes.label: def:blockmaps

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an infinite matrix over a complete ultrametric field with entries of norm $\leq 1$, unit diagonal, entries strictly below the diagonal of norm $\leq q < 1$, and finitely supported columns. Then $M$ defines an isometry of $c(\N,K)$ with dense range, hence a continuous linear equivalence.
nodes.name: Perturbed unitriangular matrices are isometries
assumptions: Let $M$ be an infinite matrix over a complete ultrametric field with entries of norm $\leq 1$, unit diagonal, entries strictly below the diagonal of norm $\leq q < 1$, and finitely supported columns
conclusions: $M$ defines an isometry of $c(\N,K)$ with dense range, hence a continuous linear equivalence
nodes.label: thm:unitriangular

nodes.statement: Norm-preservation is a largest-index argument: in $Mx$ the coordinate at the largest index where $x$ attains its norm receives the unit diagonal contribution and nothing else of that size, the sub-diagonal entries being smaller by the factor $q$. Surjectivity is $q$-adic successive approximation.
nodes.name: Proof of Perturbed unitriangular matrices are isometries
nodes.statement_short: Largest-index argument for isometry; successive approximation for surjectivity.

nodes.statement: If $AB = c\cdot 1$ then $A$ is invertible with $B = c\,A^{-1}$, $\det A\det B = c^{\,n}$, and over an algebraically closed field $(\mathrm{charpoly}\,B).\mathrm{roots} = (\mathrm{charpoly}\,A).\mathrm{roots}$ mapped by $x \mapsto c/x$.
nodes.name: Pairing of characteristic roots
assumptions: If $AB = c\cdot 1$
conclusions: $A$ is invertible with $B = c\,A^{-1}$, $\det A\det B = c^{\,n}$
nodes.label: lem:charpoly-pairing

nodes.name: Integral halo ring
nodes.statement: Let $\Lhalo = \Zp\llbracket T, pT^{-1}\rrbracket$ be the ring of \cite[Lemma 3.15]{LWX}.

nodes.name: p odd
nodes.statement: Throughout $p$ is an odd prime, so that $q = p$ in \cite{LWX}'s notation; $p = 2$ is out of scope.

$\Lhalo$ is realised coefficientwise, as \cite[proof of Corollary 3.18]{LWX} describes its elements: a two-sided stream $d : \Z \to \Zp$ with $v(d_j) \geq \max(0, -j)$, that is $\lVert d_j\rVert \leq p^{\min(0,j)}$, with pointwise addition, convolution product, and the gauge norm \[ \lVert d\rVert = \sup_{j\in\Z} \lVert d_j \rVert\, p^{-j} \in [0,1] . \]
nodes.name: Integral halo ring (coefficientwise model)
nodes.label: def:haloint

nodes.statement: The constant embedding $\Zp \to \Lhalo$ is isometric; the element $T = \delta_1$ acts as the coefficient shift and satisfies $\lVert Tx\rVert = p^{-1}\lVert x\rVert$ exactly. Consequently \[ x \in T^{k}\,\Lhalo \iff \lVert x\rVert \leq p^{-k}, \] which is \cite[Lemma 3.15]{LWX} in the only form the estimate consumes.
nodes.name: Norm of the integral halo ring
conclusions: The constant embedding $\Zp \to \Lhalo$ is isometric
x \in T^{k}\,\Lhalo \iff \lVert x\rVert \leq p^{-k}
nodes.label: prop:haloint-norm

nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a complete ultrametric field, $\psi : \Zp \to K$ an isometric ring homomorphism and $T_0 \in K$ with $p^{-1} < \lVert T_0\rVert < 1$. Then $\sum_{j\in\Z}\psi(d_j)T_0^{\,j}$ converges, and $d \mapsto d(T_0)$ is a continuous ring homomorphism $\Lhalo \to K$ satisfying $\lVert d(T_0)\rVert \leq \lVert T_0\rVert^{k}$ whenever $\lVert d\rVert\leq p^{-k}$.
nodes.name: Specialisation at a halo point
nodes.label: def:halo-specialize

nodes.statement: Inverting $T$ gives the ring $A$ of streams satisfying a \emph{shifted} halo bound. It is complete for the gauge norm, contains $\Lhalo$ isometrically as its unit ball, and $T$ is a unit with $\lVert Tx\rVert = p^{-1}\lVert x\rVert$: a multiplicative pseudo-uniformizer. So $A$ is a Banach--Tate ring in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:istate}, and every element is $T^{-k}$ times an integral one.
nodes.name: The Banach--Tate ring A = Lhalo[1/T]
conclusions: So $A$ is a Banach--Tate ring in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:istate}, and every element is $T^{-k}$ times an integral one
nodes.label: prop:halotate

nodes.statement: Write $\Zp^{\times} = \Delta \times (1+p\Zp)$, $x = \omega_{\mathrm{T}}(x)\langle x\rangle$, with the Teichm\"uller lift $\omega_{\mathrm{T}}(x) = \lim_n x^{p^n}$; let $\ell\langle x\rangle = \tfrac1p\log\langle x\rangle \in \Zp$. For a nebentypus $\omega : (\Z/p)^{\times}\to\Zp^{\times}$ the \emph{universal character} of \cite[Notation 2.1]{LWX} is \[ [x] \;=\; \omega(\bar x)\,(1+T)^{\ell\langle x\rangle} \;\in\; (\Lhalo)^{\times}, \qquad (1+T)^{s} = \sum_{r\geq 0}\binom{s}{r}T^{r} . \] It is multiplicative and takes values in the unit ball.
nodes.name: Universal character
nodes.label: def:univchar

nodes.statement: A function $f : \Zp\to\Zp$ has \emph{tilted degree $\leq n$} if $\lVert \tilde\Delta^{m}f(z)\rVert \leq p^{\,n-m}$ for all $m$ and all $z$, where $\tilde\Delta$ is the forward difference $f(z+1)-f(z)$.
nodes.name: Tilted degree
nodes.label: def:tilteddeg

nodes.statement: Tilted degree is monotone in $n$, additive under products, closed under convergent sums and pointwise limits, and constants have tilted degree $0$. The engine is the Leibniz rule $\tilde\Delta^{m}(fg) = \sum_{i+j=m}\tilde\Delta^{i}f \cdot (\tilde\Delta^{j}g)(\cdot + i)$, which is \cite[(3.5.1)]{LWX}, together with $\tilde\Delta\binom{z}{n} = \binom{z}{n-1}$, which is \cite[(3.5.2)]{LWX}.
nodes.name: The calculus of tilted degree
conclusions: Tilted degree is monotone in $n$, additive under products, closed under convergent sums and pointwise limits, and constants have tilted degree $0$
nodes.label: lem:tilted-calculus

nodes.statement: If $f : \Zp\to p\Zp$ then $z\mapsto\binom{f(z)}{n}$ has tilted degree $\leq \lfloor n/p\rfloor$; and if $g(z) = \sum_k p^{k-1}(a_k/k)z^{k}$ has the shape of a normalised logarithm then $z\mapsto\binom{g(z)}{r}$ has tilted degree $\leq 0$.
nodes.name: Tilted degree of binomial compositions
conclusions: If $f : \Zp\to p\Zp$ then $z\mapsto\binom{f(z)}{n}$ has tilted degree $\leq \lfloor n/p\rfloor$
nodes.label: lem:tilted-binomial

nodes.statement: A \emph{local matrix} is $\delta = \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c& d\end{pmatrix}\in M_2(\Zp)$ with $p \mid c$ and $d \in \Zp^{\times}$: the monoid $M_1$ of \cite[(2.3.3)]{LWX}. It has \emph{$U_p$-shape} if in addition $a \in p\Zp$, which is clause (3) of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX}.
nodes.name: Local matrix and U_p-shape
nodes.label: def:localmat

nodes.statement: \cite[Proposition 3.4]{LWX} computes the matrix of a single $\Vert_\delta$ in the Mahler basis: \[ P_{m,n}(\delta) \;=\; \tilde\Delta^{m}\Bigl(\;\binom{\tfrac{az+b}{cz+d}}{n}\,[\,cz+d\,]\; \Bigr)\Big|_{z=0} . \] Expanding $[cz+d] = [d_0](1+T)^{g(z)}$ with $g(z) = \tfrac1p\log\bigl((cz+d)/d_0\bigr)$ gives the $T$-coefficient stream $r \mapsto [d_0]\,\tilde\Delta^{m}\bigl(\binom{f(z)}{n}\binom{g(z)}{r}\bigr)\big|_{z=0}$, and we take that stream as the definition of the entry $P_{m,n}(\delta)\in\Lhalo$.
nodes.name: The entry stream
nodes.label: def:entry

nodes.statement: For a local matrix of $U_p$-shape, \[ \bigl\lVert P_{m,n}(\delta)\bigr\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-(m - \lfloor n/p\rfloor)}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad P_{m,n}(\delta) \in \mathfrak{m}^{\max(m-\lfloor n/p\rfloor,\,0)} . \] Without the shape hypothesis, that is for a general element of $M_1$, one still has $\lVert P_{m,n}(\delta)\rVert \leq p^{-(m-n)}$.
nodes.name: Entry bound
assumptions: For a local matrix of $U_p$-shape
conclusions: \bigl\lVert P_{m,n}(\delta)\bigr\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-(m - \lfloor n/p\rfloor)}
nodes.label: prop:entry-bound

nodes.statement: The $U_p$-shape makes $f(z) = (az+b)/(cz+d)$ take values in $p\Zp$, so $\binom{f(z)}{n}$ has tilted degree $\leq\lfloor n/p\rfloor$ by the first half of Lemma~\ref{lem:tilted-binomial}; $g$ is a normalised logarithm, so $\binom{g(z)}{r}$ has tilted degree $\leq 0$ by the second half; the product has tilted degree $\leq \lfloor n/p\rfloor$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tilted-calculus}, and evaluating the definition of tilted degree at the $m$-th difference and $z=0$ is the claim. The constant $[d_0]$ is a unit.
nodes.name: Proof of Entry bound
nodes.statement_short: Tilted-degree calculus for the binomial factors.

nodes.statement: A \emph{$U_p$-datum} on a class set $\iota$ consists of, for each $i\in\iota$, exactly $p$ summands, each given by a target index $\mathrm{tgt}(i,j)\in\iota$ and a local matrix $\mathrm{mat}(i,j)$ of $U_p$-shape. This is the content of \cite[Proposition 3.1]{LWX} that the estimate consumes; the column count of clause (2) is not needed. Assembling the entry streams block by block gives a matrix on $\iota\times\N$ and, by cofinite column decay, a continuous operator $D.\mathrm{op}$ on $c(\iota\times\N, \Lhalo)$.
nodes.name: U_p-datum
nodes.label: def:updatum

nodes.statement: With $t = \lvert\iota\rvert$, set $\lambda(n) = \sum_{k<n}\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)$.
nodes.name: The exponent lambda(n)
nodes.label: def:lwxlambda

nodes.statement: For every $U_p$-datum $D$ on a class set of size $t$ and every nebentypus $\omega$, the Fredholm determinant $\Char(P) = \sum_n c_n X^n$ of $D.\mathrm{op}$ is defined over $\Lhalo$ and \[ \lVert c_n\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-\lambda(n)}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad c_n \in T^{\lambda(n)}\,\Lhalo . \]
nodes.name: Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 3.16 (halo estimate)
nodes.statement_short: The Fredholm coefficients of a $U_p$-datum satisfy $c_n \in T^{\lambda(n)}\Lambda$.
assumptions: For every $U_p$-datum $D$ on a class set of size $t$ and every nebentypus $\omega$
conclusions: \lVert c_n\rVert \;\leq\; p^{-\lambda(n)}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad c_n \in T^{\lambda(n)}\,\Lhalo .
also_stated_at: On the integral model of overconvergent forms the operator $U_p$ has a matrix $P$ with entries in $\Lhalo$, and \cite[Theorem 3.16]{LWX} says that its Fredholm determinant $\Char(P) = \sum_n c_n X^n$ exists and satisfies \[ c_n \in T^{\lambda(n)}\,\Lhalo, \qquad \lambda(n) = \sum_{k<n}\Bigl(\Bigl\lfloor \tfrac{k}{t}\Bigr\rfloor - \Bigl\lfloor \tfrac{k}{pt}\Bigr\rfloor\Bigr), \] where $t$ is the size of the class set.
nodes.label: thm:lwx316

nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:entry-bound} says the matrix entry at $\bigl((i,m),(j,n)\bigr)$ has norm at most $p^{-\max(m-\lfloor n/p\rfloor,\,0)}$: a two-sided weight, with row weight $w(i,m) = m$ and column weight $w'(j,n) = \lfloor n/p\rfloor$. Lemma~\ref{lem:two-sided} therefore bounds $\lVert c_n\rVert$ by $p^{-f(n)}$ for any $f$ with $f(n)\leq \sum_{a\in S}w(a) - \sum_{a\in S}w'(a)$ over $n$-element $S$, and the combinatorial content is that $\lambda$ is such an $f$: on $\iota\times\N$ with $\lvert\iota\rvert = t$, the smallest possible value of $\sum_{(i,m)\in S}\bigl(m - \lfloor m/p\rfloor\bigr)$ over $\lvert S\rvert = n$ is attained by the first $n$ indices in the block order, which gives $\sum_{k<n}\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor \lfloor k/t\rfloor/p\rfloor\bigr) = \lambda(n)$. Summability of the minors is the same estimate. Finally $T$-divisibility is Proposition~\ref{prop:haloint-norm}.
nodes.name: Proof of Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 3.16 (halo estimate)
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided weight bound with row weight $m$ and column weight $\lfloor n/p\rfloor$, plus a block-order combinatorial minimisation.

nodes.name: Entry bound as a two-sided weight
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:entry-bound} says the matrix entry at $\bigl((i,m),(j,n)\bigr)$ has norm at most $p^{-\max(m-\lfloor n/p\rfloor,\,0)}$: a two-sided weight, with row weight $w(i,m) = m$ and column weight $w'(j,n) = \lfloor n/p\rfloor$.
nodes.statement_short: Entry bound as a two-sided weight

nodes.name: Two-sided bound and minimisation giving $\lambda$
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:two-sided} therefore bounds $\lVert c_n\rVert$ by $p^{-f(n)}$ for any $f$ with $f(n)\leq \sum_{a\in S}w(a) - \sum_{a\in S}w'(a)$ over $n$-element $S$, and the combinatorial content is that $\lambda$ is such an $f$: on $\iota\times\N$ with $\lvert\iota\rvert = t$, the smallest possible value of $\sum_{(i,m)\in S}\bigl(m - \lfloor m/p\rfloor\bigr)$ over $\lvert S\rvert = n$ is attained by the first $n$ indices in the block order, which gives $\sum_{k<n}\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor \lfloor k/t\rfloor/p\rfloor\bigr) = \lambda(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided bound and minimisation giving $\lambda$

nodes.name: Summability from the same estimate
nodes.statement: Summability of the minors is the same estimate.
nodes.statement_short: Summability from the same estimate

nodes.name: Translate to $T$-divisibility
nodes.statement: Finally $T$-divisibility is Proposition~\ref{prop:haloint-norm}.
nodes.statement_short: Translate to $T$-divisibility

nodes.statement: At a halo point $T_0$ with $p^{-1}<\lVert T_0\rVert<1$ set $\Char(P)(T_0) = \sum_n c_n(T_0)X^n \in K\llbracket X\rrbracket$. Its constant coefficient is $1$. The comparison slope sequence is $s_k = \bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)\cdot v(T_0)$, which is monotone.
nodes.name: Specialised characteristic series
nodes.label: def:speccharseries

nodes.statement: For every $T_0$ in the boundary annulus, $v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) \geq \lambda(n)\,v(T_0)$, and the Newton polygon of $\Char(P)(T_0)$ lies on or above the polygon anchored at the origin whose $k$-th unit slope is $\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)v(T_0)$.
nodes.name: Liu--Wan--Xiao Corollary 3.18 (halo lower bound)
assumptions: For every $T_0$ in the boundary annulus
conclusions: $v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) \geq \lambda(n)\,v(T_0)$
the Newton polygon of $\Char(P)(T_0)$ lies on or above the polygon anchored at the origin whose $k$-th unit slope is $\bigl(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor\bigr)v(T_0)$
also_stated_at: Specialising $T$ at a point $T_0$ of the boundary annulus $p^{-1} < \lVert T_0\rVert < 1$ gives \cite[Corollary 3.18]{LWX}: the Newton polygon of the specialised series lies on or above an explicit polygon whose slopes are the numbers $(\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor)\,v(T_0)$.
nodes.label: thm:lwx318

nodes.statement: The coefficient bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx316} pushed through the specialisation estimate of Definition~\ref{def:halo-specialize}. For the polygon statement, the constant coefficient is $1$ so the polygon is anchored at the origin, all coefficients have norm at most $1$ so the valuation sequence is admissible, and $\sum_{i<k}s_i = \lambda(k)\,v(T_0) \leq v(c_k(T_0))$ is the coefficient bound after taking logarithms; now apply the maximality clause of Definition~\ref{def:isnewtonpolygonof} to the comparison polygon of Definition~\ref{def:ofslopes}.
nodes.name: Proof of Liu--Wan--Xiao Corollary 3.18 (halo lower bound)
nodes.statement_short: Push the coefficient bound through specialisation; compare with ofSlopes polygon.

nodes.name: T-expansion coefficients b_{n,m}
nodes.statement: Write $c_n = \sum_m b_{n,m}T^{m}$ for the $T$-expansion of the integral coefficient.

$v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) = \lambda(n)v(T_0)$ if and only if $b_{n,\lambda(n)} \in \Zp^{\times}$. Otherwise there is a definite margin: \[ v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) \;\geq\; \lambda(n)\,v(T_0) + \min\bigl(v(T_0),\, 1-v(T_0)\bigr). \]
nodes.name: Equality clause of Corollary 3.18
conclusions: $v\bigl(c_n(T_0)\bigr) = \lambda(n)v(T_0)$ if and only if $b_{n,\lambda(n)} \in \Zp^{\times}$
nodes.label: thm:lwx-sharp

nodes.statement: The term-by-term estimate \cite[(3.18.1)]{LWX} shows that in $c_n(T_0) = \sum_m \psi(b_{n,m})T_0^{\,m}$ the term $m = \lambda(n)$ strictly dominates all others when $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is a unit: terms with $m < \lambda(n)$ are smaller because integrality forces $v(b_{n,m}) \geq \lambda(n)-m$, and terms with $m > \lambda(n)$ are smaller because $\lVert T_0\rVert<1$. An ultrametric sum with a unique dominant term has that term's norm. If $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is not a unit then every term loses either a factor $\lVert T_0\rVert$ or a factor $p^{-1}\lVert T_0\rVert^{-1}$, which is the stated margin.
nodes.name: Proof of Equality clause of Corollary 3.18
nodes.statement_short: Term-by-term estimate: unique dominant term iff the coefficient is a unit.

nodes.name: Term $m=\lambda(n)$ strictly dominates
nodes.statement: The term-by-term estimate \cite[(3.18.1)]{LWX} shows that in $c_n(T_0) = \sum_m \psi(b_{n,m})T_0^{\,m}$ the term $m = \lambda(n)$ strictly dominates all others when $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is a unit: terms with $m < \lambda(n)$ are smaller because integrality forces $v(b_{n,m}) \geq \lambda(n)-m$, and terms with $m > \lambda(n)$ are smaller because $\lVert T_0\rVert<1$.
nodes.statement_short: Term $m=\lambda(n)$ strictly dominates

nodes.name: Ultrametric principle
nodes.statement: An ultrametric sum with a unique dominant term has that term's norm.
nodes.statement_short: Ultrametric principle

nodes.name: Margin when not a unit
nodes.statement: If $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ is not a unit then every term loses either a factor $\lVert T_0\rVert$ or a factor $p^{-1}\lVert T_0\rVert^{-1}$, which is the stated margin.
nodes.statement_short: Margin when not a unit

nodes.statement: Conjugate the matrix $P$ by $\mathrm{diag}(T^{\lfloor n/t\rfloor - \lfloor n/pt\rfloor})$, as \cite[proof of Theorem 3.16]{LWX} does, and transpose. The result is a compactoid operator on $c(\iota\times\N, A)$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.name: Rescaled transposed halo operator
nodes.label: def:tateop

nodes.statement: Principal minors are invariant under transposition and diagonal conjugation, so the Fredholm determinant of the operator of Definition~\ref{def:tateop} is $\Char(P)$ read in $A\llbracket X\rrbracket$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.name: Determinant of the rescaled operator
conclusions: the Fredholm determinant of the operator of Definition~\ref{def:tateop} is $\Char(P)$ read in $A\llbracket X\rrbracket$
nodes.label: prop:tateop-det

nodes.statement: An index $n$ is a \emph{halo vertex} if $c_n = T^{\lambda(n)}\cdot(\text{unit})$ in $\Lhalo$. This is the situation of \cite[Remark 3.25]{LWX}; by Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx-sharp} it is implied by $b_{n,\lambda(n)}$ being a unit, that is, by the Newton polygon touching the lower bound at $n$.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.name: Halo vertex
nodes.label: def:halovertex

nodes.statement: At a halo vertex $n$, the index $n$ is dominant for $\Char(P)$ at radius $p^{\lambda(n)-\lambda(n-1)}$ and the dominant coefficient is a multiplicative unit. Hence $\Char(P) = P_n\,G$ with $\deg P_n = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:slope-factorisation}), and Theorem~\ref{thm:riesz-coleman} gives the corresponding decomposition of $c(\iota\times\N, A)$: a $U_p$-stable summand of rank $n$ carrying exactly the first $n$ slopes, over the whole boundary annulus at once.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.name: Riesz decomposition at a halo vertex
assumptions: At a halo vertex $n$
conclusions: the index $n$ is dominant for $\Char(P)$ at radius $p^{\lambda(n)-\lambda(n-1)}$ and the dominant coefficient is a multiplicative unit
nodes.label: thm:halo-riesz

nodes.statement:
Dominance at the stated radius is convexity of $\lambda$: the increments $\lfloor k/tfloor - \lfloor k/ptfloor$ are non-decreasing, so $\lambda(k) - k
u$ is minimised at $k = n$ for $
u$ the $n$-th increment, and the inequality is strict beyond $n$ because the increments grow. The coefficient bound of Theorem~ef{thm:lwx316} gives the inequality for $k 
eq n$ and the vertex hypothesis gives equality at $n$ together with multiplicativity of the norm on $c_n$, since $\lVert TVert$ is multiplicative and units of $\Lhalo$ are detected by their leading coefficient. Now apply Theorem~ef{thm:slope-factorisation} and then Theorem~ef{thm:riesz-coleman}.
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex
nodes.name: Proof of Riesz decomposition at a halo vertex
nodes.statement_short: Convexity of $\lambda$ gives dominance; then slope factorisation and Riesz--Coleman.

nodes.name: Dominance from convexity of $\lambda$
nodes.statement: Dominance at the stated radius is convexity of $\lambda$: the increments $\lfloor k/t\rfloor - \lfloor k/pt\rfloor$ are non-decreasing, so $\lambda(k) - k\nu$ is minimised at $k = n$ for $\nu$ the $n$-th increment, and the inequality is strict beyond $n$ because the increments grow.
nodes.statement_short: Dominance from convexity of $\lambda$
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex

nodes.name: Coefficient bound and vertex hypothesis
nodes.statement: The coefficient bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx316} gives the inequality for $k \neq n$ and the vertex hypothesis gives equality at $n$ together with multiplicativity of the norm on $c_n$, since $\lVert T\rVert$ is multiplicative and units of $\Lhalo$ are detected by their leading coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient bound and vertex hypothesis
nodes.section: 10.7 Riesz theory at a halo vertex

nodes.name: Apply slope factorisation and Riesz--Coleman
nodes.statement: Now apply Theorem~\ref{thm:slope-factorisation} and then Theorem~\ref{thm:riesz-coleman}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply slope factorisation and Riesz--Coleman

nodes.statement: Over a complete ultrametric field $K$ with $\lVert p\rVert<1$ and $p$ odd, $\log u = \sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^{n}\tfrac{(u-1)^{n+1}}{n+1}$ for $\lVert u-1\rVert<1$ and $\exp w = \sum_n w^{n}/n!$ for $\lVert w\rVert^{2}<\lVert p\rVert$. On the joint disc they are mutually inverse, and $\log$ is additive.
nodes.name: p-adic exponential and logarithm
nodes.label: def:padicexplog

nodes.statement: For $e, x \in K$ with $\lVert x\rVert\leq c$, $\lVert e\rVert\lVert x\rVert\leq c$ and $c^{2}<\lVert p\rVert$, \[ \sum_{r\geq 0}\binom{e}{r}x^{r} \;=\; \exp\bigl(e\log(1+x)\bigr). \]
nodes.name: The p-adic binomial theorem at an arbitrary exponent
assumptions: For $e, x \in K$ with $\lVert x\rVert\leq c$, $\lVert e\rVert\lVert x\rVert\leq c$ and $c^{2}<\lVert p\rVert$
conclusions: \sum_{r\geq 0}\binom{e}{r}x^{r} \;=\; \exp\bigl(e\log(1+x)\bigr)
nodes.label: thm:padic-binomial

nodes.statement: Fix $x$ and regard both sides as power series in the exponent $e$, with geometrically decaying coefficients. They agree at every $e = n \in \N$, by the finite binomial theorem on the left and $\exp(n\log u) = u^{n}$ on the right. A power series vanishing at all natural numbers vanishes identically, by Strassman's theorem applied along $p^{k}\to 0$.
nodes.name: Proof of The p-adic binomial theorem at an arbitrary exponent

nodes.statement: Both sides of the identity are continuous in $u$ and agree on $\N$, where they are the ordinary binomial theorem, and $\N$ is dense in $\Zp$. nodes.statement: The specialisation of the universal character at $T_0$ is $\kappa_{T_0}(x) = \omega(\bar x)\,(1+T_0)^{\ell\langle x\rangle} = \omega(\bar x)\exp\bigl(s\log\langle x\rangle\bigr)$, with halo exponent $s = \log(1+T_0)/p$. On the sub-annulus $p^{-1}<\lVert T_0\rVert$, $\lVert T_0\rVert^{2}<p^{-1}$ it is an analytic weight in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:analyticweight}: the group is $\psi(\Zp^{\times})(1+p\calO_K)$, the level is the image of $M_1$, and the expansion of $\kappa_{T_0}(cz+d)$ on the closed unit ball is \[ (cz+d)^{2}\,\kappa_{T_0}(d)\sum_{m\geq 0}\binom{s}{m}\Bigl(\frac{c}{d}\Bigr)^{m}z^{m}, \qquad \text{decay } \rho = \lVert T_0\rVert\sqrt{p} . \]

nodes.statement: With $h = m-1$, $T'_h = (1+T_0)^{p^{h}}-1$ and $s_h = \log(1+T'_h)/p^{h+1}$, the character on the disc of radius $p^{-(h+1)}$ about a $\Zp$-unit $a$ is $x\mapsto [a](T_0)\exp\bigl(s_h\log(x/a)\bigr)$, an analytic weight at the level $M_1^{(h)}$ of matrices with $p^{h+1}\mid c$, of radius $\max(p^{-(h+1)}, \lVert T'_h\rVert)\sqrt p$.

nodes.statement: Mahler's theorem applies because $\Lhalo$ is an ultrametric $\Zp$-Banach algebra. Change of coordinates from the Colmez basis to the monomial basis is an isometry with dense range, hence a continuous linear equivalence, and \[ \mathrm{monomialToMahler} \;=\; \mathrm{diag}(m!)\circ\mathrm{colmezEquiv}^{-1} . \]

nodes.statement: Let $g_n = \lfloor n/p^{h}\rfloor!\binom{z}{n}$ and let $a < p^{h}$ be a disc centre. The polynomial $g_{n,a}(w) = g_n(a+p^{h}w)$ has $\Zp$-coefficients, and factors as $g_{n,a} = c_{n,a}f_{n,a}$ where $f_{n,a}$ reduces mod $p$ to a monic polynomial of degree $\lvert K_{n,a}\rvert$, $K_{n,a} = \{k<n : k\equiv a \pmod{p^{h}}\}$, and $v(c_{n,a}) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{h}[\,a \bmod p^{\ell} < n\bmod p^{\ell}\,] \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Colmez's Lemme 1.4.9
conclusions: The polynomial $g_{n,a}(w) = g_n(a+p^{h}w)$ has $\Zp$-coefficients

nodes.statement: Each linear factor $a-k+p^{h}w$ is $p^{h}(w-(k-a)/p^{h})$ when $p^{h}\mid k-a$, and otherwise $(a-k)\bigl(1+p^{h}w/(a-k)\bigr)$; collecting the two kinds of factor gives the factorisation, and the valuation of the scalar is the count of carries, which is the displayed sum.

nodes.name: Proof of Colmez's Lemme 1.4.9
nodes.statement_short: Factor each linear factor and count carries.

nodes.statement: Model $\mathcal{O}B_{p^{-h}}$, the functions analytic on every disc $a+p^{h}\Zp$ with the maximum of the $p^{h}$ Gauss norms, by $c(\Z/p^{h}\times\N, K)$ --- the Taylor coefficients on each disc in the coordinate $z = a+p^{h}w$. Then the map sending $e_n$ to the disc model of $g_n$ is an isometric equivalence $c(\N,K) \to c(\Z/p^{h}\times\N,K)$, and composing with $\mathrm{diag}(\lfloor n/p^{h}\rfloor!)$ turns Colmez coordinates into Mahler coefficients.

nodes.statement: Order the basis by $n = (m(n)+1)p^{h} - i(n)$ with $1\leq i(n)\leq p^{h}$, and the discs by their centres, as \cite{Colmez} does; in that order Lemma~\ref{lem:colmez-valuation} says the reduction of the basis-change matrix is block upper triangular with each diagonal block lower triangular with invertible diagonal entries. Reindexing the columns by the involution reversing each block of $p^{h}$ consecutive integers turns the matrix into a perturbed unitriangular one, so Theorem~\ref{thm:unitriangular} applies. The two reindexings cancel, so the resulting map sends $e_n$ to $g_n$ on the nose. The final clause is the level-$h$ form of the statement that Mahler coefficients are forward differences of values at $\N$-points.

nodes.statement: The action (2.3.2) does not preserve a single disc: it \emph{permutes} the discs. Writing $t_a(w) = a+p^{h}w$ and $a' = \delta(a)\bmod p^{h}$, the matrix identity $\delta\, t_a = t_{a'}\,\delta'$ with $\delta' = t_{a'}^{-1}\delta t_a$ of level $h$ says that the action carries the Taylor expansion on $a'$ to the one on $a$ through the single-disc weight action of Definition~\ref{def:haloweighth}. So the disc action is a block operator of $\kappa$-slashes permuted by $a\mapsto a'$, and it is a right action because the two data satisfy the cocycle rules. Everything in Chapter~\ref{chap:qmf} then transcribes: the space $S^{D,\dagger,m}$, evaluation at representatives, the Hecke operator, its compactness, its Fredholm determinant, and the eigenvalue reading of the zeros.

nodes.statement: Four steps. (iv) Basis independence (Theorem~\ref{thm:charpowerseries-inv}) gives $\det(1-XP') = \det(1-X[U\eta U])$.

That conjecture has three clauses: sufficiently close to the boundary, \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{Spc}^{>r}_D$ is a disjoint union of countably many connected components $Z_n$, each finite and flat over the annulus $\mathcal{W}^{>r}$ via the weight map; \item there are rationals $\alpha_1 \leq \alpha_2 \leq \cdots \to \infty$ with $\lvert a_p(z)\rvert = \lvert T_{\mathrm{wt}(z)}\rvert^{\alpha_n}$ for $z \in Z_n$; \item the sequence $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots$ is a disjoint union of \emph{finitely many arithmetic progressions}, counted with multiplicity (at least for large indices).

In \cite{LWX}'s normalisation $\mathrm{slopeRatio}(j) = \varphi(q)\,\tilde\alpha_j(\omega)$, the factor $\varphi(q)$ of (1.5.1) being absorbed into our ratio and $\tilde\alpha$ being the sequence $\alpha$ repeated according to the degrees $\deg Y_{i,\omega}$.

nodes.statement: The Newton polygon of $\Char(P)(T)$ is the convex hull of the points $(n, v(c_n(T)))$. Thus the two hulls agree after scaling by $v(T)$, and reading unit slopes off a scaled polygon multiplies them by the same scalar.

nodes.name: Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 1.5 (spectral halo)
nodes.statement: Let $\omega : \Delta \to \Zp^{\times}$ be a character. Then there exists $\lambda \in (0,1)$ such that there exists a sequence of rational numbers $\alpha_0(\omega), \alpha_1(\omega), \dots$ in increasing order and tending to infinity such that $\mathrm{Spc}^{>\lambda}_{D,\omega}$ is a disjoint union $\coprod_{i\geq 0} Y_{i,\omega}$ of rigid analytic spaces finite and flat over $\mathcal{W}^{>\lambda}_\omega$ via $\mathrm{wt}$, such that \[ v\bigl(a_p(y)\bigr) = \varphi(q)\,v\bigl(T_{\mathrm{wt}(y)}\bigr)\,\alpha_i(\omega) \tag{1.5.1} \] for every $y \in Y_{i,\omega}$. More precisely, if the tame level is neat, then we can take $\lambda = p^{-8/((p^{2}-1)t+8)}$ for $p > 2$ \dots \emph{Moreover}, let $M$ be a positive integer so that $p^{-q/p^{M-1}(p-1)} > \lambda$ \dots Then if we extend the sequence $\alpha_0(\omega), \alpha_1(\omega),\dots$ into $\tilde\alpha_0(\omega), \tilde\alpha_1(\omega), \dots$ with each $\alpha_i(\omega)$ appearing with multiplicity $\deg Y_{i,\omega}$, then $\tilde\alpha_0(\omega), \tilde\alpha_1(\omega), \dots$ is a disjoint union of $(p-1)p^{M-1}t/2$ arithmetic progressions with (the same) common difference $\varphi(q)p^{M}/2q^{2}$. More precisely, \[ \tilde\alpha_{j + q^{-1}p^{M}t}(\omega\omega_0^{2}) = \tilde\alpha_j(\omega) + \frac{p^{M}}{q^{2}} \qquad\text{for any } j \geq 0. \tag{1.5.2} \]
nodes.section: 12.5 What Theorem 1.5 says, and what \S4 proves
nodes.statement_short: Over a small boundary annulus the spectral curve is a disjoint union of finite flat pieces with $a_p$-slopes $v(T)$ times fixed rationals forming arithmetic progressions.

nodes.statement: Let $\omega$ be a character of $\Delta$, $\omega_0$ the Teichm\"uller character and $k \geq 0$, and let $(k,\psi)$ be a classical weight on the disc $\omega$, so that $\psi|_\Delta = \omega\omega_0^{-k}$. The \emph{conjugate} nebentypus is $\omega^{-1} : u \mapsto \omega(u)^{-1}$; the \emph{partner} nebentypus $\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2k}$ is the disc of the Atkin--Lehner partner $(k,\psi^{-1})$; and the \emph{target} nebentypus $\omega\omega_0^{-2k-2}$ is the disc of the theta target $(-k-2,\psi)$. Since every statement of Chapters~\ref{chap:lwx-halo}--\ref{chap:lwx-slopes} is proved for an arbitrary $\omega$, these further instances cost nothing, and the same $U_p$-datum serves all of them, the nebentypus entering only through the entry streams.
nodes.name: Conjugate, partner and target nebentypi
nodes.label: def:conjchar

nodes.statement: The element $w = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-p^{m}&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $p^{m}$, normalises the Iwahori subgroup, inverts the nebentypus, and conjugates $U_p$ to $U'_p$ --- all expressed by the inverse-free identity $w\,\gamma^{w} = \gamma\,w$. \emph{Granting} the operator identity $U_p\circ U'_p = p^{k+1}$ on the classical space, Lemma~\ref{lem:charpoly-pairing} gives \cite[Proposition 3.22]{LWX}: the $U_p$-slopes at nebentypus $\psi$ and at $\psi^{-1}$ pair up to $k+1$.
nodes.name: Atkin--Lehner, reduced
conclusions: the $U_p$-slopes at nebentypus $\psi$ and at $\psi^{-1}$ pair up to $k+1$
nodes.label: prop:atkin-lehner

nodes.statement: \emph{Atkin--Lehner data} of conductor $p^{h+1}$ at a nebentypus $\psi$ consist of a section $\iota_p : \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p) \to G$ of the $p$-component such that the level contains the lifts of the Iwahori subgroup, the central element $p$ at $p$ is a global central element times an element of the level, and the Atkin--Lehner element of level $p^{h+1}$ normalises the disc-$0$ part of the level; together with a Hecke character restricting to $\psi$ on the level. A \emph{family} of such data is a single section with a Hecke character for every disc $\omega$ and every weight $k$. The $U_p$-representatives are built from the section alone, so one $U_p$-datum serves every classical weight of the family at once.
nodes.name: Adelic Atkin--Lehner data
nodes.label: def:al-data

nodes.statement: Grant Atkin--Lehner data of conductor $p^{h+1}$ at $\psi$. On the classical forms $S^{D}_{k+2}(K^{p}\Iw_{p^{h+1}};\psi)$ --- in the disc model, the forms with values in the locally polynomial functions of degree $\leq k$ --- the Atkin--Lehner element induces an isomorphism $W$ onto the classical forms at $\psi^{-1}$, and \[ U_p \circ W^{-1} \circ U_p^{(\psi^{-1})} \circ W \;=\; p^{k+1} . \] Hence the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:atkin-lehner} holds at the classical points, and the $U_p$-slopes at $\psi$ and at $\psi^{-1}$ pair up to $k+1$.
nodes.name: The Atkin--Lehner identity
assumptions: Grant Atkin--Lehner data of conductor $p^{h+1}$ at $\psi$
conclusions: U_p \circ W^{-1} \circ U_p^{(\psi^{-1})} \circ W \;=\; p^{k+1} .
nodes.label: prop:al-identity

nodes.statement: Expand the composite over the coset representatives of $U_p$. The term with trivial representative is central and contributes $p^{k+1}$. After conjugation by the Atkin--Lehner element every other term is a sum of the nebentypus over the cosets of $1 + p^{h+1}\Zp$ in $1 + p^{h}\Zp$, which vanishes because the conductor is exactly $p^{h+1}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:atkin-lehner} then gives the pairing.

nodes.statement: In the disc model an element \emph{is} the family of Taylor coefficients on each disc, so $\theta^{r}$ --- $r$-fold differentiation, \cite[\S7]{Bu04} --- is the shift $(a,j)\mapsto (j+1)\cdots(j+r)\,c(a,j+r)$: a diagonal of integers composed with a shift, bounded by $1$ and column-finite, hence continuous, and block-diagonal over the discs. Its kernel at $r = k+1$ is exactly the locally polynomial functions of degree $\leq k$, which is the first sentence of \cite[Proposition 4]{Bu04}, of dimension $(k+1)p^{h}$ per disc --- the local half of \cite[(3.21.1)]{LWX}. If the automorphy factors of two weights have the classical shape of exponent $k$ and the target shape of exponent $k+2$, with the same constants, then $\theta^{k+1}$ intertwines $U_p$ at the first weight with $p^{k+1}U_p$ at the second.
nodes.name: The theta operator and the classical subspace
conclusions: Its kernel at $r = k+1$ is exactly the locally polynomial functions of degree $\leq k$
nodes.label: prop:theta

nodes.statement: At the classical point of weight $k$ on the disc $\omega$, the Fredholm determinant of $U_p$ on the complement of the classical subspace equals the Fredholm determinant of $p^{k+1}U_p$ at the theta target $(-k-2,\psi)$, a halo point on the disc of the target nebentypus $\omega\omega_0^{-2k-2}$.

nodes.statement: Let $T_0$ be the classical point of a weight $(k,\psi)$ with $\psi$ of conductor $p^{2}$, and suppose that the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:atkin-lehner} holds between $T_0$ and its Atkin--Lehner partner. Then the Newton polygon of $\Char(P)(T_0)$ passes through $\bigl(n_{k+1}, \lambda(n_{k+1})v(T_0)\bigr)$; hence $\mathrm{HasUnitBand}(k+1)$.

assumptions: Let $T_0$ be the classical point of a weight $(k,\psi)$ with $\psi$ of conductor $p^{2}$

nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-factor} the characteristic series at $T_0$ is the determinant of the complement times the reversed characteristic polynomial of $U_p$ on the classical subspace, of dimension $n_{k+1} = (k+1)pt$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:theta}; so the height of the polygon at $n_{k+1}$ is at most $v(\det U_p)$ on that subspace, and the same holds at the partner point. The hypothesis gives $v(\det U_p) + v(\det U'_p) = n_{k+1}(k+1)v(p) = 2\lambda(n_{k+1})v(T_0)$, the partner point having the same norm as $T_0$. With the lower bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx318} at both points, both inequalities are equalities, and Lemma~\ref{lem:unitband-from-touching} converts touching into $\mathrm{HasUnitBand}(k+1)$.

nodes.statement: At $k = 0$ the band is automatic. For $k+1$, the classical point of weight $k$ on the disc $\omega$ lies in the halo, and Proposition~\ref{prop:al-identity} at the member of the family of weight $k$ on the disc $\omega$ supplies the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx-stepone} there; the $U_p$-datum does not depend on $(\omega,k)$ because the family has a single section.

nodes.statement: Let $r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega)$ be the largest index $d$ such that the $d$-th coefficient of the characteristic series on the disc $\omega$ is a unit of the halo ring; it is at most $t$. With $\deg X_{k,\omega} = n_k^{+} - n_k^{-}$ and $\deg X_{(k,k+1),\omega} = n_{k+1}^{-} - n_k^{+}$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor:lwx13-slopes}, $\deg X_{0,\omega} = r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega)$; and, granted a family of Atkin--Lehner data of conductor $p^{2}$, for every disc $\omega$ and every $n \geq 0$ \[ \deg X_{n+1,\omega} = r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2n}) + r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega\omega_0^{-2n-2}), \qquad \deg X_{(n,n+1),\omega} = pt - r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2n}) - r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega\omega_0^{-2n}) \;>\; 0 . \]
nodes.name: Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 1.3, the degrees
conclusions: $\deg X_{0,\omega} = r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega)$
nodes.label: thm:lwx13-degrees

nodes.statement: At $n_{k+1}$ the unit band splits the degree into the left gap $n_{k+1} - n_{k+1}^{-}$ and the right gap $n_{k+1}^{+} - n_{k+1}$, and the finite factor splits the polygon: the classical slopes are at most $(k+1)v(p)$ and those of the complement at least $(k+1)v(p)$. The left gap counts the classical slopes equal to $(k+1)v(p)$; the Atkin--Lehner pairing of Proposition~\ref{prop:al-identity} matches them with the classical slopes $0$ at the partner point, which are all its ordinary slopes, so the left gap is $r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2k})$. The right gap counts the slopes of the complement equal to $(k+1)v(p)$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:theta-exact} these are the ordinary slopes of the theta target, so the right gap is $r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega\omega_0^{-2k-2})$. The interval degrees are $pt$ minus the two gaps at consecutive vertices, an exact subtraction because $n_k^{+} \leq n_{k+1}^{-}$; positivity is $r_{\mathrm{ord}} \leq t$ with $p \geq 3$.

nodes.statement_short: Split degrees into gaps; Atkin--Lehner pairing and theta sequence identify gaps.

nodes.name: Split into left and right gaps
nodes.statement: At $n_{k+1}$ the unit band splits the degree into the left gap $n_{k+1} - n_{k+1}^{-}$ and the right gap $n_{k+1}^{+} - n_{k+1}$, and the finite factor splits the polygon: the classical slopes are at most $(k+1)v(p)$ and those of the complement at least $(k+1)v(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Split into left and right gaps

nodes.name: Left gap via Atkin--Lehner pairing
nodes.statement: The left gap counts the classical slopes equal to $(k+1)v(p)$; the Atkin--Lehner pairing of Proposition~\ref{prop:al-identity} matches them with the classical slopes $0$ at the partner point, which are all its ordinary slopes, so the left gap is $r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2k})$.
nodes.statement_short: Left gap via Atkin--Lehner pairing

nodes.name: Right gap via theta sequence
nodes.statement: The right gap counts the slopes of the complement equal to $(k+1)v(p)$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:theta-exact} these are the ordinary slopes of the theta target, so the right gap is $r_{\mathrm{ord}}(\omega\omega_0^{-2k-2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Right gap via theta sequence

nodes.name: Interval degrees and positivity
nodes.statement: The interval degrees are $pt$ minus the two gaps at consecutive vertices, an exact subtraction because $n_k^{+} \leq n_{k+1}^{-}$; positivity is $r_{\mathrm{ord}} \leq t$ with $p \geq 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Interval degrees and positivity

nodes.statement: Granted a family of Atkin--Lehner data of conductor $p^{2}$, $\deg X_{I,\omega} = \deg X_{I+1,\omega\omega_0^{2}}$ for $I = (0,1), 1, (1,2), 2, \dots$, and hence $\deg X_{I,\omega}$ is periodic in $I$, on the same range, modulo $\varphi(q)/2 = (p-1)/2$.

nodes.statement: Substitute $(n,\omega) \mapsto (n+1,\omega\omega_0^{2})$ in the formulas of Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx13-degrees}: the partner and target nebentypi of Definition~\ref{def:conjchar} do not change. Iterate, and use $\omega_0^{p-1} = 1$.
nodes.name: Proof of Liu--Wan--Xiao Corollary 1.4

nodes.statement: Let $h \geq 1$ satisfy $(p^{2}-1)t + 8 < 8p^{h-1}(p-1)$, and grant families of Atkin--Lehner data of conductors $p^{2}$ and $p^{h+1}$ over a single section. Then for every disc $\omega$, every $k \geq 0$, every $i < N = t(k+1)p^{h}$ and every $j \geq 0$, \begin{align*} \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2k}}(N-1-i) + \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega}(i) &= (k+1)\,p^{h-1}(p-1), \\ \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega\omega_0^{2}}(j + p^{h}t) &= \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega}(j) + p^{h-1}(p-1), \\ \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega}\bigl(j + \tfrac{p-1}{2}\,p^{h}t\bigr) &= \mathrm{slopeRatio}_{\omega}(j) + \tfrac{p-1}{2}\,p^{h-1}(p-1). \end{align*} With $M = h+1$ and $\mathrm{slopeRatio} = \varphi(q)\tilde\alpha$, the second line is (1.5.2), and the third says that $\tilde\alpha_0(\omega), \tilde\alpha_1(\omega), \dots$ is a disjoint union of $(p-1)p^{M-1}t/2$ arithmetic progressions with common difference $\varphi(q)p^{M}/2q^{2}$.
nodes.name: Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 1.5, second half, at the polygon level
assumptions: Let $h \geq 1$ satisfy $(p^{2}-1)t + 8 < 8p^{h-1}(p-1)$
nodes.label: thm:lwx152

nodes.statement: At a classical point of conductor $p^{h+1}$ in the slope-reading region, the classical subspace carries exactly the first $N$ slopes: they are at most $(k+1)v(p)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:al-identity} and $\lVert U_p\rVert \leq 1$, while those of the complement are at least $(k+1)v(p)$, through the theta target. The Atkin--Lehner pairing reverses them against the partner nebentypus, which with (1.5.1) at both discs (Theorem~\ref{thm:lwx-unitband}) is the first line. The first line at $(\omega,k)$ and at $(\omega,k+1)$, subtracted, is \cite[(4.2.5)]{LWX}; taking the disc $\omega^{-1}\omega_0^{2k}$ gives (4.2.6), the second line; and $\omega_0^{p-1} = 1$ iterates it into the third.
nodes.name: Proof of Liu--Wan--Xiao Theorem 1.5, second half, at the polygon level
nodes.statement_short: Classical subspace carries first $N$ slopes; Atkin--Lehner reversal; subtract and iterate.
